item.title: The Detective's Maxim: A Victorian Cryptogram
item.description:
You spot a two-letter word that starts with the free T. It has to be TO. You fill in the O, and suddenly an eight-letter word reads T _ _ O _ _ _ _ and your brain refuses to let it go. Five minutes later you’re muttering at a 135-year-old sentence about evidence. That’s the cryptogram effect: one right guess pays for itself everywhere the letter appears.

Every letter in the quote below has been swapped for a different letter, and the swap holds for the whole puzzle. If K means E once, it means E every time. No letter ever stands for itself. You get one letter free.

item.title: A Day in the Armchair: A Sherlock Holmes Cryptogram
item.description:
Watson comes home from his club after a wet day, and Holmes tells him exactly where he’s been. Watson concedes it’s “rather obvious”. Holmes, who has been sitting in the same armchair since breakfast surrounded by tobacco smoke, uses the moment to say something about how blind everybody else is. It’s one sentence. Holmes would like you to notice it.

This cipher is shorter than the easy ones, and short quotes are harder. There’s less text to compare, and fewer repeats to lean on. Every letter is swapped for a different one, the swap holds throughout, and one letter is given to you free. Make it work for its keep.

item.title: The Prefect's Problem: An Edgar Allan Poe Cryptogram
item.description:
The Prefect of the Paris police has taken a minister’s apartment apart. He’s probed the cushions with needles, checked the rungs of every chair and examined the floor with a microscope. Three months in, he drops into a chair in Dupin’s darkened library and admits the case is simple, and he’s still beaten. Dupin, smoking in the dark, offers one quiet suggestion. The Prefect laughs at him.

Poe created his detective more than forty years before Holmes, and he knew his ciphers too: “The Gold-Bug” turns on one. This quote is a single sentence. Every letter is swapped for a different one, the swap holds throughout, and one letter is given away.

item.title: Detective Clues: A Murder Mystery Connections Puzzle
item.description:
You see SCARLET, MUSTARD, PLUM and BLUE, and you’re already reaching for the Submit button. Four colours, done. Except PEACOCK is sitting two tiles over, smirking. Now you have five candidates for four slots, one mistake on the board, and a creeping suspicion that this puzzle was written by someone who enjoys watching you squirm. It was.

The rules are short. Sixteen words hide four groups of four. Pick four you think belong together and submit. Find all four groups before you make four mistakes.
